notesMap.2026-08-03:
Go doesn't have classes or inheritance — it uses composition and interfaces to achieve the same encapsulation and polymorphism goals. A struct only declares data; methods are attached externally via a receiver, not inside the type definition. And unlike a PHP object (passed by reference), a struct is passed by value by default — assigning it or passing it as an argument creates a copy, unless you use a pointer

Como funciona controle de acesso/visibilidade em Go?
In Go, visibility doesn't use keywords like public/private — it's determined by the first letter of the identifier. Uppercase means exported, visible outside the package; lowercase means unexported, only accessible within the same package. This applies equally to structs, fields, functions, and variables

Por que módulos em Go usam nomes tipo github.com/usuario/repo?
The module name acts as a globally unique namespace, usually based on the Git repository path. This avoids naming collisions between different people's modules, and it means the module is already ready to be imported by others via go get, even if it's only used locally today.

Como Go implementa encapsulamento sem private/public?
Encapsulation in Go happens at the package level, not the struct level. Exported fields and methods (capitalized) are visible outside the package; unexported ones (lowercase) are only accessible within the same package — including by other structs in that package. This means that to enforce a business rule around access to some data, you keep the field unexported and expose only controlled methods, typically from a different package than the consuming code.
notesMap.2026-08-06:
Qual seu processo pra debugar erros em Go?
I compile frequently, every few lines, instead of writing everything and testing at the end — that takes advantage of Go catching most type errors at compile time. I read the error message top to bottom, fix one issue at a time, and recompile. For errors the compiler won't catch — like using the wrong API call — I use editor autocomplete to see what's actually available on a type or interface, and check the official docs at pkg.go.dev.
notesMap.2026-08-07:
Go treats errors as ordinary values, returned explicitly, instead of a separate control-flow mechanism like try/catch. The core justification isn't that exceptions lack flexibility — it's visibility: with throw, an error can silently jump across several functions up the call stack, and you can't tell just from a function's signature whether it might fail. Errors as values force explicit handling right at the point where the problem occurs. Go still has panic/recover, but it's reserved only for truly exceptional situations — bugs, not everyday expected errors.

O que acontece se você passar errors.As com um target do tipo valor, quando o Error() tem receiver ponteiro?
It compiles fine, because errors.As takes the target as any, with no compile-time type checking. But it panics at runtime, because errors.As requires the type pointed to by target to itself implement the error interface — and since Error() has a pointer receiver, only the pointer type implements that interface, not the value type

Qual a diferença entre errors.Is e errors.As?
I use Is when I want to know whether a specific sentinel error is present anywhere in the chain — it's an identity comparison. I use As when I know there's a custom error type in the chain and I want to extract that specific instance, to access its own fields, not just the generic error interface message
notesMap.2026-08-11: I use Unmarshal when the data already arrives as []byte from something outside my control — a literal string in a test, the return value of another function, data embedded via go:embed. In those cases there's no real stream to take advantage of, so wrapping the bytes in a Reader just to use Decoder would be unnecessary work. Whenever I control how the source is read — a file, a request body — I prefer Decoder from the start, via os.Open or r.Body, since it processes incrementally without requiring everything in memory at once.
notesMap.2026-08-08:
ListenAndServe accepts the connection and spins up a dedicated goroutine for it. The ServeMux matches method and path against registered routes and dispatches to the right handler. Inside the handler, path parameters and the request body are extracted and validated, with client errors returning 400 immediately. Business logic runs against the application state, and the response is built by setting the status code and Content-Type before encoding and writing the body


Quando você usa %w vs %v ao formatar um erro?
I use %w when the error will keep existing as a Go value that other code further up the call stack might want to inspect with errors.Is or errors.As. I use %v when I'm just formatting the error for final display — logging, on-screen text, or an HTTP response to an external client — because in those cases the error has already reached the end of the line as a Go value; what comes out is just text.
notesMap.2026-08-09:
Por que usar %q em vez de %v ao comparar strings num teste?
%q wraps the string in quotes and makes special characters visible, so subtle differences — like a trailing space or a hidden newline — become obvious in the failure message. With %v, two strings that look identical but are technically different can mislead whoever's reading the failing test.


It needs to be in a file with a name like xxx_test.go

The test function must start with the word Test

The test function takes one argument only t *testing.T

To use the *testing.T type, you need to import "testing", like we did with fmt in the other file


Por que extrair valores literais para constantes nomeadas, em vez de usá-los diretamente no código?
It avoids 'magic strings/numbers' scattered through the code — values that, if mistyped somewhere, the compiler won't catch, since it's technically just another valid string. Centralizing them in a named constant gives you a single source of truth and communicates the value's meaning to whoever reads the code. The practical rule is: if a value appears more than once, or represents something with business meaning, it's worth extracting; if it's an isolated, non-reused value, it usually isn't

Por que resetar estado global no início de cada teste?
Because package-level variables persist across tests in the same process — Go doesn't automatically reset that state between runs. Without an explicit reset, a test can pass or fail depending on what order other tests ran before it, which breaks the independence a good test needs to have.
notesMap.2026-08-13:
Table-driven tests centralize the verification logic in one place, and each new scenario just becomes a line of data in the table instead of a whole duplicated test function. That reduces repetition and makes it easy to add new cases. But it's only worth it when there are actually multiple real scenarios going through the same logic — forcing the format onto a single case adds structure without benefit, so the decision to use table-driven should come from real scenario variation, not from following a pattern for its own sake

notesMap.2026-08-10: It was a philosophical decision, not a limitation. Go was built for large-scale infrastructure systems at Google, prioritizing simplicity and explicitness over the implicit conventions and reflection-heavy magic that traditional frameworks tend to rely on. The standard library already ships with an HTTP server, routing, and JSON parsing — enough for most use cases — and the Go community culture favors composing small, focused libraries over adopting one big framework that decides everything for you.
notesMap.2026-08-14: Three main things: first, shared state — the tasks slice — being accessed by multiple goroutines with no synchronization at all, which is a race condition waiting to happen under load. Second, the use of global variables instead of dependency injection — this doesn't just couple the code together, it's already showing up as real pain in the tests, which have to manually reset state on every run, something that wouldn't be necessary if the state were encapsulated in a struct passed in explicitly. Third, the server doesn't handle OS interrupt signals, so a deploy or restart could drop requests mid-processing instead of waiting for them to finish.
notesMap.2026-08-15:
In Eloquent, Task::create() hides SQL generation, field mapping, and fetching the generated ID behind a single call — it's an ORM, built for productivity through convention. In Go, using database/sql without an ORM, every step is explicit: I write the exact SQL that will run, pass parameters positionally to prevent SQL injection, and use Scan to capture the result back into the struct. It's more verbose, but it removes any hidden 'magic' — what runs against the database is exactly what's written in the code, with no translation layer in between. It's the same explicitness philosophy that shows up in Go's native routing, without a framework: less automatic abstraction, more direct control.

Como parâmetros posicionados previnem SQL injection?
With positional parameters, the query and the values are sent to the database separately — the SQL structure is fixed upfront, and values are always treated as literal data, never as executable code, even if the content looks like SQL syntax. Concatenating strings directly eliminates that separation: everything becomes a single SQL string, and the database has no way to distinguish malicious input from legitimate command.
notesMap.2026-08-17:
Because there's no guaranteed order between goroutines — the Go runtime's scheduler decides when each one runs, mapping goroutines onto a smaller number of OS threads, and those threads in turn compete for CPU time with other processes on the machine. Since those factors vary on every run, the result is non-deterministic: without explicit synchronization, you should never assume a specific execution order between goroutines


Qual a diferença entre concorrência e paralelismo em Go?
Concurrency is about structuring a program into parts that make progress independently — it's a design decision in the code. Parallelism is about those parts actually running at the same physical instant, on different CPU cores — it's an execution concern, decided by the runtime and available hardware. Go has native support for concurrency through goroutines, and the runtime may or may not exploit real parallelism under the hood depending on how many cores are available — but that's not something the programmer controls or should assume as guaranteed.
notesMap.2026-08-18: The WaitGroup's internal counter never reaches zero, so wg.Wait() blocks forever. If, at that point, every goroutine in the program is blocked — none of them making progress — the Go runtime actively detects that state and kills the program with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!', instead of letting the process hang silently forever.
notesMap.2026-08-19: Because an unbuffered channel has no internal space to hold values — it doesn't store, it only transports. That forces the send and the receive to happen at the exact same instant, a mechanism called a rendezvous: whoever sends blocks until there's someone on the other side ready to receive at that same moment. That makes the channel, by itself, a synchronization tool, not just a way to exchange data — unlike a buffered channel, which lets you send without waiting, until the buffer fills up.
notesMap.2026-08-20: When there's a real speed difference between producer and consumer, a small buffer limits how far ahead the producer can get before blocking, effectively forcing both sides to run at the slower one's pace — even if the producer alone would be much faster. That's dangerous because it produces no error at all, it just silently wastes real parallelism capacity, and it can lead to misdiagnosing the wrong component as the bottleneck, since the apparent slowness comes from the buffer size, not the producing logic.

Goroutine 9 (finished) created at: ... main.go:15 — mesma coisa pra goroutine 9, só que essa já tinha terminado (finished) quando o conflito foi reportado — o que é normal: a race foi entre a escrita dela (já concluída) e a escrita da goroutine 11 (ainda rodando), sem barreira de sincronização entre as duas.

exit status 66 — código de saída do processo, diferente de zero, sinalizando falha — é assim que ferramentas de CI/CD automatizadas sabem que devem bloquear um deploy se -race encontrar qualquer problema (muitos times configuram go test -race como parte obrigatória do pipeline, justamente por causa disso).

Que tipos de acesso concorrente configuram uma data race?
Simultaneous reads by multiple goroutines are never a problem, as long as no write is involved — data that isn't changing can be read by as many goroutines as you want, at the same time, safely. The problem shows up when at least one of the concurrent accesses is a write, whether that's a write racing another write, or a write racing a read — in either case, without explicit synchronization, the result becomes unpredictable
notesMap.2026-08-22:
Because a cache, by its typical usage pattern, is read far more often than it's written to — the whole point of a cache is avoiding recomputing or refetching an expensive value repeatedly. RWMutex lets multiple reads happen truly in parallel, without blocking each other, and only forces full exclusion when a write is involved. In a read-heavy scenario like this, that drastically cuts down on unnecessary serialization that a plain Mutex would otherwise impose, even between operations that have no real conflict with each other


Por que capturar a variável do loop diretamente em uma goroutine podia causar bug em versões antigas de Go?
Before Go 1.22, the for loop reused the same iteration variable across every pass — any goroutine created inside the loop captured, via closure, a reference to that same shared variable, not its own value. Since goroutines run asynchronously, it was common for the loop to have already moved on by the time the goroutine actually read the variable, causing multiple goroutines to read the same final value, or unexpected values. The fix was passing the variable in as a function argument, creating a fresh copy at the moment the goroutine was launched. Since Go 1.22, each iteration already creates a new variable automatically, so that protective pattern is no longer strictly necessary, but it's still important to recognize in legacy code.
notesMap.2026-08-23: An unbuffered jobs channel feeds a fixed number of worker goroutines, each in a range loop waiting for work. A separate goroutine produces the jobs and closes the channel when done. Results go into a second channel, consumed continuously by the caller — never read in a batch at the end. A dedicated goroutine waits for the WaitGroup to confirm every worker has finished, and only then closes the results channel, letting the consumer use a simple range loop to read until the end, without needing to know the result count upfront
notesMap.2026-08-24: The worker now has two possible event sources instead of one — a new job, or a cancellation signal — and reacts to whichever becomes ready first, instead of getting stuck waiting indefinitely for work that might never arrive. This solves a real problem that a manual check at the top of the loop wouldn't: if the worker is blocked receiving from a channel, a context error check at the start of the iteration would never be reached. Putting ctx.Done() as a select case ensures cancellation is observed even while the worker is waiting for work.
notesMap.2026-08-25:
Por que chamar cancel() mesmo quando o contexto já tem um timeout configurado?
WithTimeout creates an internal timer in the runtime, scheduled to fire when the deadline expires. If the operation finishes before that and nobody calls cancel() manually, that timer keeps existing, holding onto resources, until the timeout completes on its own — it's a temporary leak, not a permanent one, but an avoidable one. Calling cancel() as soon as the operation finishes releases that timer immediately, instead of relying on the timeout to expire by itself. In a system handling many concurrent operations, each creating its own context, skipping this piles up unnecessary pressure on the runtime.
